title: Simplex, Duality and Sensitivity Analysis
subject: LIT 803
description: Twenty-five questions across easy, medium and hard on the Simplex method, primal and dual problems, the duality theorems and sensitivity analysis.

questions.prompt: Who developed the Simplex Method?
questions.explanation: It is an iterative algebraic algorithm.

questions.prompt: Where does the Simplex Method typically start?
options: At an initial feasible vertex, typically the origin
questions.explanation: It then moves along edges to adjacent corners, improving Z at each step.

questions.prompt: What is the mirror formulation of a linear program called?
questions.explanation: The original problem is the Primal.

questions.prompt: What do dual variables (shadow prices) measure?
options: The marginal worth of extra units of system resources
The total cost of the firm
questions.explanation: This is the economic interpretation of duality.

questions.prompt: What does the Strong Duality Theorem say?
options: Z is always greater than W
If either problem has an optimal solution, both do, and Max Z = Min W
questions.explanation: The optimal objective values of the Primal and the Dual are equal.

questions.prompt: What does the Weak Duality Theorem say?
options: Z(X*) ≥ W(Y*) for any feasible pair
For feasible solutions, Z(X*) ≤ W(Y*) when the Primal is a maximisation problem
Z(X*) = W(Y*) for any feasible pair
Only optimal solutions can be compared
questions.explanation: Any feasible primal value is a lower bound on any feasible dual value.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of sensitivity analysis?
options: To convert a problem to standard form
To see how an optimal solution changes when inputs vary, without resolving the problem from scratch
questions.explanation: It is also called post-optimality analysis.

questions.prompt: Which three types of change does the sensitivity section study?
options: Objective coefficients, technological coefficients and right-hand-side values
questions.explanation: These are the cⱼ, aᵢⱼ and bᵢ values of the model.

questions.prompt: Why can solving the Dual be faster than solving the Primal?
options: The Dual has more constraints, so it is more accurate
The Dual never needs standard form
A Primal with many constraints and few variables has a Dual with few constraints and many variables, needing fewer Simplex iterations
The Dual always has a smaller objective value
questions.explanation: Simplex effort depends largely on the number of constraints.

questions.prompt: In a maximisation Primal, what kind of dual variable goes with a ≤ constraint?
questions.explanation: An equality constraint gives an unrestricted dual variable.

questions.prompt: What kind of dual variable goes with an equality constraint in the Primal?
questions.explanation: That is why Y₂ is unrestricted in the worked example.

questions.prompt: When converting a maximisation Primal to its Dual, what happens to the objective coefficients cⱼ?
options: They become the dual objective coefficients
They become the right-hand-side limits of the dual constraints
questions.explanation: The Primal right-hand sides bᵢ become the dual objective coefficients.

questions.prompt: What does the Unboundedness Theorem say?
options: If one problem is unbounded, the other is also unbounded
If one problem is unbounded, the other is infeasible
questions.explanation: This links the behaviour of the Primal and the Dual.

questions.prompt: What does the Complementary Slackness Theorem say?
options: At the optimum, each variable multiplied by its corresponding slack is zero
All variables are positive at the optimum
questions.explanation: In symbols, Xⱼ* × (Dual Slackⱼ) = 0 and Yᵢ* × (Primal Slackᵢ) = 0.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, which dual constraint belongs to X₂ (coefficients 2 and −1)?
questions.explanation: The columns of the Primal become the rows of the Dual, and the sign is ≥ because X₂ ≥ 0.

questions.prompt: In the sensitivity base model Max Z = 100X₁ + 80X₂, what is the optimal point and value?
If the unit profit of X₁ rises from ₦100 to ₦120, what happens to the optimum?
options: It stays at C(60, 40), and Z becomes ₦10,400
questions.explanation: The new slope of −1.5 still lies within the range for which C is optimal.

questions.prompt: What is the dual objective for the primal Max Z = 5X₁ + 12X₂ + 4X₃ with right-hand sides 10 and 8?
questions.explanation: The right-hand sides become the dual objective coefficients, and the goal changes to minimisation.

questions.prompt: A primal problem has 3 variables and 2 constraints. How many variables and constraints does its dual have?
questions.explanation: Primal variables become dual constraints, and primal constraints become dual variables.

questions.prompt: In the sensitivity base model, which two constraints meet at the optimum C(60, 40)?
questions.explanation: Resources 2 and 3 meet at (53.3, 53.3), which breaks constraint 1.

questions.prompt: At C(60, 40), how much of resource 3 (X₁ + 2X₂ ≤ 160) is left unused?
questions.explanation: Use is 60 + 2(40) = 140, so 160 − 140 = 20 units are left.

questions.prompt: For the objective Z = c₁X₁ + 80X₂, the optimum stays at C(60, 40) while the objective line slope is in which range?
questions.explanation: C lies between constraint 1 (slope −1) and constraint 2 (slope −2). So c₁ must be between ₦80 and ₦160.

questions.prompt: When resource 2 usage for X₂ falls so that constraint 2 becomes 2X₁ + (2/3)X₂ ≤ 160, what is the new optimum?
options: E(70, 30) with Z = ₦9,400, where the new constraint 2 meets X₁ + X₂ = 100
questions.explanation: With X₂ = 100 − X₁, 2X₁ + (2/3)(100 − X₁) = 160 gives X₁ = 70. The point (64, 48) breaks constraint 1.

questions.prompt: When resource 3 drops from 160 to 120, what is the new optimum?
questions.explanation: G is where 2X₁ + X₂ = 160 meets X₁ + 2X₂ = 120. The profit is (20,000 + 6,400)/3 = 8,800.

questions.prompt: A dual problem is solved and its optimal objective value is ₦500. What is the optimal objective value of the primal?
questions.explanation: By strong duality, the optimal values are equal.
